title: Past-Future Scheduler for LLM Serving under SLA Guarantees
problem: LLM serving frameworks using continuous batching suffer from either overestimation of memory consumption (conservative schedulers) or underestimation leading to harmful request evictions (aggressive schedulers), because neither accurately accounts for the dynamic memory release profile of concurrently running requests across future decoding steps.
motivation: As LLM inference scales to thousands of GPUs serving tens of millions of requests per day under strict SLA constraints (TTFT, TPOT, MTPOT), maximizing goodput (SLA-satisfying throughput) requires precise KV-cache memory estimation that adapts to varying input-output length distributions across chatbot, code, and reasoning workloads.
method: The Past-Future scheduler predicts how long each request's output will be by examining the actual lengths from the last ~1,000 completed requests, then continuously updates this prediction as each request generates more text. It then calculates memory usage at every future point when requests finish, and finds the maximum memory needed across all those future moments. A new request is only accepted if adding it keeps the peak future memory below the hardware's capacity. LightLLM implements this with less than 1% scheduling overhead by running the calculations in parallel on the GPU.
key_novelty: Output lengths from AI models are stable enough within short time periods that the scheduler can predict peak future memory needs precisely by sampling from historical request data, without requiring model-specific tuning.
contributions: Discovery that LLM request output length distributions are stable within adjacent time windows, validated on six real-world trace datasets including BurstGPT and Mooncake.
Past-Future scheduler: a two-component algorithm estimating future peak memory via historical output length distribution sampling and per-future-completion-event memory accounting.
LightLLM: a production-deployed LLM serving framework implementing the Past-Future scheduler on a cluster of thousands of GPUs.
2-3x higher goodput than vLLM (aggressive) and TGI/DeepSpeed-MII (conservative) schedulers under heavy load across Llama2-7B, 13B, 70B models on A100, H800, and 4090 hardware.

metrics.speedup: 2-3x higher goodput over aggressive/conservative schedulers under heavy load
metrics.other: Memory utilization approaches theoretical optimum (93-94% vs 98% oracle) while eviction rate drops to ~3-7% vs 93% for aggressive at watermark=99%; 50-60% throughput improvement on multimodal LLaVA and Qwen-VL models

limitations: The scheduler relies on distribution stationarity within adjacent time windows and may perform poorly if output length distributions shift abruptly (e.g., sudden workload type change); warm-up period needed at service startup.
primary_theme: history-aware future memory estimation for LLM serving scheduler goodput
